1.q: ק֚וּם רִ֣יב אֶת־הֶ⁠הָרִ֔ים וְ⁠תִשְׁמַ֥עְנָה הַ⁠גְּבָע֖וֹת קוֹלֶֽ⁠ךָ
1.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commands me to arise and contend before the mountains, and to let the hills hear my voice]

Yahweh is saying what he wants the hills to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants to happen. Alternate translation: [the hills should be able to hear]
The pronoun **your** refers to Micah, the prophet whom Yahweh is commanding to speak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your voice, Micah]

2.q: שִׁמְע֤וּ הָרִים֙ אֶת־רִ֣יב יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠הָ⁠אֵתָנִ֖ים מֹ֣סְדֵי אָ֑רֶץ
2.note: Micah is speaking to the **mountains** and the **foundations of the earth**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about everything in all creation hearing the case that Yahweh is bringing against them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the mountains and the foundations of the earth. Alternate translation: [Let all creation hear the dispute of Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dispute**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh as he disputes]

The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh, and the phrase **his people** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [with the Israelites, his people]

2.q: כִּ֣י רִ֤יב לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עִם־עַמּ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל יִתְוַכָּֽח
2.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh has a dispute that he is bringing against his people, Israel]

Micah is using **a dispute is to Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh has a dispute.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has a dispute with his people]

3.note: This verse begins a direct quotation from Yahweh that continues through verse 5. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as modeled in the UST.

Yahweh is using the question form to assert that he has done nothing to harm his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have done nothing to harm you or to burden you!]

By **Testify against me**, Yahweh is using the language of a court and saying that if they actually have anything to accuse him of, they should testify. The implication from the previous questions is that they have nothing to accuse him of. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Only if I have done anything wrong can you testify against me]

4.note: Yahweh is speaking of Egypt as if it had been a **house** where people kept **slaves.** Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and from where you were held as slaves]

Here, **to your face** represents “before you” or “ahead of you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [ahead of you]

5.q: זְכָר & מַה־יָּעַ֗ץ בָּלָק֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ מוֹאָ֔ב וּ⁠מֶה־עָנָ֥ה אֹת֖⁠וֹ בִּלְעָ֣ם בֶּן־בְּע֑וֹר
5.note: Yahweh assumes that readers will know that he is referring to the events describe in Numbers 22-24. The phrase **what Balak, king of Moab, counseled** refers to his plot to destroy Israel by hiring Balaam to curse them and **what Balaam, son of Beor, answered him** refers to the fact that Balaam told the king he could only bless the people rather than curse them. You could include this information in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

The implication is that Yahweh wants his people to remember what happened to their ancestors when they were able to miraculously cross the Jordan River (see Joshua 3 and 4). **Shittim** was the location of their last camp east of the Jordan River, and **Gilgal**, was where first camped in the land that he had promised them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and remember what I did for your ancestors when they crossed the Jordan River]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousnesses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how Yahweh acted righteously toward you]

6.note: This verse begins a shift from Yahweh’s words to the direct quotation spoken by a worshiper who represents the people. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating this shift in speaker.

To **bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [worship the God of]

The speaker is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [With what shall I bow down]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **God** that is characterized by **the height**, that is, by his exalted position. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the exalted God]

The speaker is using **calves, sons of a year** as a common expression of the culture to mean “calves that are one year old.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with calves that are one year old]

7.note: The speaker says **thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [an enormous number of rams, with an unimaginable amount of oil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the ways I have rebelled]

Here the speaker is speaking of a child who came from his own body as if it were **the fruit of my belly**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my own child that I fathered]

8.note: In this verse the speaker changes, as Micah answers the questions that the previous speaker has asked. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating a change of speaker in your language.
The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has told]

Micah is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [human being]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right and fair]

Micah is using the possessive form to describe a **love** that is characterized as **covenant faithfulness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and love faithfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and faithfully loving others]

Here Micah is speaking of how one lives as if it were **to walk** down a path and by **with your God**, he means that one should live one’s whole life in fellowship with God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to be humble as you live your whole life in fellowship with your God]

Micah is using the possessive form **your God** to mean that Yahweh is the God whom the people worship, not that they possess or control him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom you worship]

9.note: The phrase **The voice of Yahweh** represents the message that Yahweh speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The message that Yahweh speaks]

Here, **the city** represents the people who live in the city of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of the city]

Micah has been speaking to the people about Yahweh, but here he briefly turns aside and addresses Yahweh directly. He does this in order to express more powerfully his own reverence for Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could introduce this more clearly and put the rest of this address in quote marks. Alternate translation: [and I say to Yahweh, “Sound wisdom fears your name”]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sound wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and whoever is truly wise]
Here, **your name** represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you yourself]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and whoever Yahweh appointed]

The phrase **and whoever he appointed** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Scholars have proposed, however, that the first word of the next verse should actually belong to this verse, and that the letters of the words have been divided incorrectly in the present text. By adding the first word of verse 10 to this phrase, changing two letters in it, and dividing the words differently, the meaning would be as in this alternate translation. You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and the assembly of the city]

10.q: ע֗וֹד הַ⁠אִשׁ֙ בֵּ֣ית רָשָׁ֔ע אֹצְר֖וֹת רֶ֑שַׁע וְ⁠אֵיפַ֥ת רָז֖וֹן זְעוּמָֽה
10.note: Yahweh is using the question form to accuse the people of the city of cheating others in their business dealings. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There are still in the house of the wicked treasuries of wickedness, and the ephah of leanness that is cursed!]

The phrase **Are there still** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. The wording in the text, however, is very unusual, and scholars have proposed that the first word should be read with the previous verse and that a letter has dropped off of the second word. Reading the text in this way results in the following alternate translation. You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Can I forget]

Yahweh is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the person who is wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things gained wickedly]

This **ephah** was equivalent to 22 liters or nearly two thirds of a bushel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an **ephah** that is characterized by **leanness**, that is, a measure that holds less than it should. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the undersized ephah]

The expression **is cursed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that I, Yahweh, have cursed]

11.q: הַ⁠אֶזְכֶּ֖ה בְּ⁠מֹ֣אזְנֵי רֶ֑שַׁע וּ⁠בְ⁠כִ֖יס אַבְנֵ֥י מִרְמָֽה
11.note: Yahweh is using the question form to declare that no one who uses dishonest weights and measures can be innocent. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly would not be innocent if I used scales of wickedness and a bag of stones of deceit!]

The phrase **Would I be innocent** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. It would also be possible to read the word as “Would I acquit.” You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Would I acquit someone]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **scales** that are used for **wickedness** or cheating people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with unjust scales]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **stones**, which were used to weigh things they were selling, that are characterized by **deceit** because they were the wrong weight. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceitful stones]

12.note: The words **which** and **her** refer to the city that Yahweh mentioned in verse 9. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [—the city whose rich]

Yahweh is using the adjective **rich** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [her rich people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent acts]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. You could use the approach which is modeled in the UST of connecting the phrases with a word other than “and” that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and all her inhabitants speak deceitfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [her inhabitants speak falsely]
Here, **tongue** represents speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and what they say is deceitful]

13.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will make** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself is the one who will act. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And even I, myself will make sick]

Yahweh is using **make sick the striking of you** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he will administer an incurable injury on them. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will strike you with an incurable wound]

The pronouns **you** and **your** from here to the end of the chapter refer to the people of the city of Jerusalem whom Yahweh is now addressing directly after speaking about them in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the striking of you, inhabitants of Jerusalem]

14.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will eat** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between the heavenly Judge and the sentence they will suffer. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For your part, you will eat]

The word **dysentery** refers to a kind of disease of the bowels that empties the body of the food it takes in. If your readers would not be familiar with what dysentery is, you could use the name of a similar sickness that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [because your stomach will be empty]

The word translated as **bring to safety** could also be the word for “reach.” This leads some scholars to interpret these sentences in the context of birthing rather than warfare. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [And you will reach birth, but not deliver the baby]

Here, **the sword** represents warfare and being killed in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will hand over to be killed in war]

15.q: אַתָּ֥ה תִזְרַ֖ע וְ⁠לֹ֣א תִקְצ֑וֹר אַתָּ֤ה תִדְרֹֽךְ
15.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verbs translated as **you will sow** and **you will tread** already include this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how the people will suffer. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You people of the city will certainly sow, but not reap, and you will certainly tread]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and you will tread new wine grapes but not drink wine]

16.note: The expression **are kept** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For the people keep the statutes of Omri]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the statutes that Omri established. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the statutes that Omri established]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of the deeds of the house of Ahab are kept]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Ahab** figuratively means all the people descended from that evil king as modeled in the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the descendants of Ahab were a **house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Ahab]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if living according to the advice of Omri and Ahab were to have **walked in their counsels**. He is referring to the corrupt policies, economic injustice, and foreign idol worship (like Baal worship) institutionalized by Omri and his son, Ahab (see 1 Kings 16). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have followed their advice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [desolate]
The pronoun **her** refers to the city that Yahweh mentioned in verse 9. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the inhabitants of that city]

Here, **a hissing** represents the scorn that people will express toward those who live in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and her inhabitants an object of scorn]
